meaning: Informal shorthand for thanks. Quick, light acknowledgement used widely in texting and instant messaging.

by_scene.work: Acceptable between peers and reports in chat; too casual for clients or seniors in most workplaces.
by_scene.romance: Very common at all stages.
by_scene.friends: Very common.
by_scene.family: Common between siblings; unlikely from parents or elders.

examples.reading: Quick, friendly acknowledgement between colleagues.
Casual thanks to a partner; ordinary.
Grateful acknowledgement between friends.

meaning: Asks the other person to inform the speaker about something. Leaves the next step with the reader.

by_scene.work: Common between peers. Clients may find it too casual. Can function as a soft nudge when paired with a time.
by_scene.romance: Common. Can read as laid-back or as leaving the ball in the other person's court.
by_scene.friends: Very common.
by_scene.family: Common between siblings; less likely from elders.

examples.text: lmk when you're free this week
examples.reading: Casual request for availability; neutral.

examples.text: lmk if you want to come
examples.reading: Open invitation; no pressure.
Shows interest without being pushy.

meaning: Signals that the speaker is being candid. Often precedes an opinion the speaker thinks may be unwelcome or surprising. Can soften a disagreement or preface criticism.

by_scene.work: Uncommon in formal contexts; used between close peers. Can precede a frank opinion.
by_scene.romance: Common. Often precedes a vulnerable statement or a complaint.
by_scene.friends: Very common. Marks frankness.
by_scene.family: Used between siblings; rare from elders.

examples.text: tbh I think we should scrap the whole approach
examples.reading: Frank disagreement softened by the opener.

examples.text: tbh I was a bit hurt by that
examples.reading: Honest expression of feelings; the abbreviation lowers the formality of the admission.

examples.text: tbh I forgot you even asked
examples.reading: Blunt admission; casual tone keeps it light.

meaning: Emphasises that the speaker is being honest, often before something surprising or slightly uncomfortable. More emphatic than tbh.

by_scene.work: Too casual for most work contexts; occasionally between very close peers.
by_scene.romance: Common, especially at earlier stages. Can precede a compliment or a concern.
by_scene.friends: Very common. Often precedes a surprising opinion.
by_scene.family: Used between siblings; very unlikely from parents.

examples.reading: Blunt feedback between peers; the opener signals honesty rather than malice.

examples.text: ngl I really like talking to you
examples.reading: A step toward expressing feelings; the abbreviation keeps it casual.

examples.text: ngl I thought you were going to cancel again
examples.reading: Frank remark about a pattern; could be playful or pointed depending on context.

meaning: A conversation opener or check-in. Asks what the other person is currently up to. Often a prelude to making a plan or starting a chat.

by_scene.work: Very rare; too casual even between close peers in most settings.
by_scene.romance: Common at all stages. At just_connected or talking it can be a bid for attention.
by_scene.friends: Very common as a conversation starter.
by_scene.family: Used between siblings; unlikely from parents.

examples.reading: Checking availability; likely leading to a plan.
Casual opener; wants to chat or make a plan.

meaning: Signals the speaker is stepping away briefly and will return. Sets an expectation of continued conversation.

by_scene.work: Acceptable between peers in instant messaging; not used in email or with clients.
by_scene.romance: Common. Polite signal that the speaker is not ignoring the other person.
by_scene.friends: Very common.
by_scene.family: Used between siblings; parents may not know the term.

examples.reading: Quick explanation for a pause; considerate.
Brief absence; no concern.

meaning: Withdraws a question, request, or topic. Can be neutral or can signal frustration or resignation, depending on context and whether the speaker adds anything else.

by_scene.work: Occasionally between peers. Can read as passive-aggressive if used after a request was ignored.
by_scene.romance: Common. After a request or suggestion, it can signal hurt or withdrawal. Followed by silence it reads as displeasure.
by_scene.friends: Common. Usually neutral between close friends; can signal annoyance if curt.
by_scene.family: Used between siblings; unlikely from elders.

examples.reading: Withdrawing the request; could be neutral self-sufficiency or mild frustration.
Abrupt withdrawal; likely signals frustration or hurt, especially after being ignored.
Resolved their own question; neutral.

meaning: Expresses uncertainty or indifference. Can be genuine uncertainty, deflection, or a signal that the speaker does not want to engage with the question.

by_scene.work: Too casual for most work contexts; occasionally between close peers.
by_scene.romance: Common. As a response to a direct question, it can read as evasive or disengaged.
by_scene.friends: Very common. Usually genuine.
by_scene.family: Used between siblings; from a teenager to a parent it can signal unwillingness to discuss.

examples.reading: Noncommittal; low engagement; gives the other person nothing to work with.

examples.text: idk ask Sophie she was there
examples.reading: Genuine uncertainty; redirects helpfully.
Struggling to articulate a feeling; genuine rather than dismissive.

meaning: Originally literal laughter but now mostly a softener or filler. Signals the speaker is being light or playful. Rarely means actual laughter; for that, speakers tend to repeat it or use other markers. Can deflect seriousness.

by_scene.work: Used between close peers in chat; too casual for clients or seniors.
by_scene.romance: Very common. Softens a message. Overuse can read as nervous. After a serious statement it may be deflecting.
by_scene.friends: Very common. Part of casual register.
by_scene.family: Used between siblings. Some parents have adopted it; from an elder it can read as trying to be approachable.

examples.reading: Amused reaction; the lol confirms it is a joke, not a complaint.
Light apology; the lol downplays the missed messages.

examples.text: lol I have no idea what you just said
examples.reading: Friendly admission of confusion; keeps the tone light.

meaning: Bare acknowledgement. Its reading depends heavily on the relationship and the moment. At work and in family chats with elders, it is a neutral, efficient reply. In romance, especially after a disagreement or at a stage where engagement is expected, it can signal displeasure or low interest.

by_scene.work: Neutral acknowledgement. No tone reading. Equivalent to Noted. or Got it.
by_scene.romance: At just_connected or talking: low engagement; gives the other person nothing to respond to. At dating or established: possible displeasure, especially after a disagreement. At ex_friends or ex_distant: neutral.
by_scene.friends: At new or regular: neutral. At close: neutral unless right after a disagreement, where it may signal displeasure.
by_scene.family: From a parent or elder: neutral; elders write short. Between siblings: neutral unless right after a disagreement.

examples.reading: Simple acknowledgement; no tone reading.
Very short; after a plan or request it can signal displeasure or indifference.
Neutral; elders write short messages. No tone reading.

meaning: Refers the reader back to a previous message. In workplace culture it is widely understood as a signal of impatience: the speaker feels they already provided the information or made the request, and the other person missed it or ignored it.

by_scene.work: Between any colleagues or external contacts. Polite on the surface but often signals frustration. A first use is a reference; a second use is a clear cue.
by_scene.romance: Not used.
by_scene.friends: Not used.
by_scene.family: Not used.

examples.text: Per my last email, the deadline was moved to Friday.
examples.reading: Pointing out that this was already communicated; likely impatient.

examples.text: Per my last email, I do need the signed copies before we can proceed.
examples.reading: Formal reminder to a client; polite but firm, with an edge of impatience.

meaning: Asks the reader for guidance or a decision. Common in workplace email and messaging. Can feel cold or demanding when used without context, as it puts all responsibility on the reader.

by_scene.work: Common in formal messages, especially to seniors or clients. Between peers it can feel stiff. After a list of problems it can read as pressure.
by_scene.romance: Not used.
by_scene.friends: Not used.
by_scene.family: Not used.

examples.text: The supplier has not confirmed the order and we are two days from the deadline. Please advise.
examples.reading: Escalating a problem to a senior; the phrase puts the decision squarely on the reader.

examples.text: Please advise on how you would like to proceed.
examples.reading: Formal request for direction; neutral and professional.

meaning: A follow-up message. The first use is genuinely neutral. A second or third use on the same topic signals growing impatience, as the speaker implies the reader has not responded to earlier messages.

by_scene.work: Common between all relationship types. A single use is polite; repeated use is a pressure cue. Combined with a deadline it becomes more pointed.
by_scene.romance: Not typically used in this form; would sound formal.
by_scene.friends: Occasionally used; sounds more formal than typical friend register.
by_scene.family: Occasionally used by parents or elders checking on the user.

examples.text: Just checking in on the status of the report.
examples.reading: A polite follow-up; neutral on first use.

examples.text: Just checking in again. Do you have an update?
examples.reading: Second follow-up; the word again signals the speaker has been waiting.

meaning: Refers to a prior conversation or agreement. Often used to hold the reader to something they said or agreed to. Can be a neutral reference or a way of closing off further discussion.

by_scene.work: Common in follow-up messages. Neutral when confirming action items. Can be pointed when the speaker feels the reader is not honouring the agreement.
by_scene.romance: Not used in this form.
by_scene.friends: Not used.
by_scene.family: Not used.

examples.text: As discussed, I'll need the final version by end of play Wednesday.
examples.reading: Confirming a deadline that was previously agreed; neutral but firm.

examples.text: As discussed, this is outside our current scope.
examples.reading: Holding a boundary with a client; references a prior agreement to strengthen the position.

meaning: A follow-up on a previous request or deadline. The word friendly is meant to soften the reminder, but repeated use undercuts the friendliness. A third use is almost universally read as impatience.

by_scene.work: Common in workplace messages. First use is genuinely soft. Second use is firmer. Third use is a clear impatience signal.
by_scene.romance: Not used.
by_scene.friends: Not used.
by_scene.family: Not used.

examples.text: Friendly reminder that the expense forms are due by Friday.
examples.reading: First use; genuinely polite.

examples.text: Friendly reminder that I still need your section for the deck.
examples.reading: Repeated use; the word still makes the impatience visible.

meaning: Acknowledges receipt of information without committing to action or expressing an opinion. At work it is efficient and neutral. In personal contexts it can read as cold or dismissive because it gives nothing back.

by_scene.work: Neutral acknowledgement from any relationship type. No tone reading.
by_scene.romance: Unusual and likely to read as cold or passive-aggressive, especially at dating or established.
by_scene.friends: Unusual; would read as formal and distant.
by_scene.family: From a parent or elder: neutral, similar to Ok. Between siblings: reads as cold.

examples.reading: Efficient acknowledgement; no tone reading.
Acknowledges the information; neutral.
Feels cold and dismissive; likely signals displeasure.

meaning: Informal British closing or expression of thanks. Equivalent to thanks or bye. Very common in UK workplace messages between peers and sometimes with clients. Also used as a standalone thanks in everyday speech.

by_scene.work: Very common as a sign-off in UK workplaces. Friendly but professional. Less formal than Regards or Kind regards.
by_scene.romance: Uncommon as a closing in romantic contexts; would read as distant or jokey.
by_scene.friends: Common as thanks between UK friends.
by_scene.family: Common as thanks or bye between UK family members.

examples.text: I'll send that across now. Cheers
examples.reading: Friendly sign-off confirming an action; professional and warm.
Casual thanks; very natural in UK English.

meaning: Informal British term of address, equivalent to buddy or pal. Used between friends, colleagues of similar status, and sometimes with strangers in casual contexts. Can carry warmth, solidarity, or mild confrontation depending on tone.

by_scene.work: Common between UK peers; would be inappropriate to a senior or client.
by_scene.romance: Rarely used between romantic partners; more likely in friend-zone contexts or as a joke.
by_scene.friends: Very common between UK friends; increasingly used regardless of gender.
by_scene.family: Between siblings; unlikely from parents to children.

examples.reading: Warm thanks between UK colleagues.
Casual greeting; very common in UK English.
Expressing disapproval; mate here adds familiarity, not friendliness.

meaning: Very informal British English for thanks. Shorter and more casual than cheers. Common in northern England and among older speakers. Younger speakers in some regions also use it. Usage varies a lot by region and age.

by_scene.work: Occasionally between close UK peers; too informal for most workplaces.
by_scene.romance: Uncommon in romantic texts; would read as very casual or regional.
by_scene.friends: Used between UK friends, especially in northern England.
by_scene.family: Common from UK parents and grandparents; natural in family texts.

examples.reading: Affectionate thanks from a parent; very natural in northern UK English.
Quick, casual thanks between close UK friends.

meaning: American slang for agreement or acknowledgement, similar to sure, sounds good, or OK. Originally from African American Vernacular English, now widespread among younger American speakers. Usage varies a lot by age and region.

by_scene.work: Too casual for most workplaces; occasionally between young peers in informal settings.
by_scene.romance: Used by younger speakers to confirm a plan or agree. Casual and warm.
by_scene.friends: Very common among younger American speakers as a quick agreement.
by_scene.family: Between younger siblings; unlikely from parents.

examples.reading: Confirming a plan; enthusiastic agreement.
Quick agreement; engaged and positive.
